column17: The paper designs, instantiates and evaluates an artefact: a two-phase formative study with five domain experts yields four challenges (C1-C4), three findings (F1-F3) and seven design requirements (DR1-DR7), from which the SCSimulator system (backend LLM-driven MAS pipeline + predictive/XAI modules + five-view frontend) is built and then demonstrated via a usage scenario and evaluated in a technical evaluation and a user study (Sections 3-7). Stated contributions are the design requirements, the tool, and its demonstration. Not purely conceptual (a working system exists) and not primarily empirical data collection about a phenomenon.
column19: A working, deployed system is described in detail (four-stage LLM agent pipeline with full prompts in Appendix A; VGAE + regression SC Explain Model; Horizon Extend Model; SHAP; five interactive views) and is evaluated quantitatively: link-prediction ACC/Precision/Recall/F1 against observed network evolution plus Gwet's AC1 and firm-level consistency ratios across three backbone LLMs over 80 independent runs (Table 1), an expert-based Likert evaluation of agent behaviour with ten participants (Table 2), and a user study with 12 participants reporting NASA-TLX, usability and effectiveness scores (Table 5). BORDERLINE: the authors explicitly position the tool as a 'proof-of-concept' and heuristic/exploratory rather than predictive system, report no baseline comparison, and describe their validation as qualitative ('while SCSimulator demonstrates clear potential for qualitative validation, ... scaling toward quantitative robustness remains a central challenge', p. 1619). 'prototype' is therefore defensible; coded 'implemented-validated' because working system + quantitative metrics are both present. R1 decision needed.
column20: Manufacturing, specifically the paper products / paper and paperboard packaging sector and its upstream and downstream supply chain; framing is B2B manufacturing supply chains generally (footnote 1, p. 1603). Formative-study experts: three senior managers from manufacturing enterprises, two SCM academics.
column21: Supplier-customer partner selection in the paper packaging supply chain. Evaluation dataset: 35 anonymized firms observed over eight quarters (2023-2024), edges from public tendering/bidding records (cebpubservice.cn, gsxt.gov.cn), node attributes from public firm profiles, with temporal attributes expert-scored on a normalized 0-100 scale along Operation, Technology and Reputation. Usage scenario: manager 'Alice' at Company-4838, an incumbent paper-products firm facing green-economy entrants 6174 and 7437, explores customer diversification into specialty food and cultural products over Q8-Q13.
column22: NR (no numbered research questions). The paper instead states three challenges to address - (1) representing dynamic relationships, (2) revealing agent reasoning and impact, (3) balancing adaptive autonomy with expert intervention (Section 1, p. 1603) - and three contributions: deriving seven design requirements for SC partner selection with domain experts, introducing SCSimulator as an interactive visual analytics tool providing multi-faceted interpretability and intervention mechanisms, and demonstrating effectiveness and reliability via a usage scenario and a user study (p. 1604).
column24: The planning object is the configuration of the supply chain network itself: which upstream suppliers and downstream customers a focal firm is linked to, with the underlying mechanism explicitly framed by the authors as 'edge formation and deletion in social networks' (Section 8.3, p. 1620). Partner selection is presented as 'a typical multi-objective dynamic game problem, which integrates the core principles from Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and Game Theory (GT)' (p. 1603). BOUNDARY CASE: the paper contains no facility location, capacity, site, factory-layout or technology-investment content, so no second subdomain is coded; 'logistics-distribution-network-design' does not fit because no flows, distribution structures or logistics assets are modelled - only inter-firm relationship structure. The controlled vocabulary has no 'supplier/partner selection' subdomain, which is the paper's actual topic; SC-network-design is the nearest scoped term.
column29: No planning time horizon is stated anywhere. The only temporal specifications are data/simulation granularity: the dataset covers eight quarters (2023-2024), Alice sets 'both the reference window and simulation turn length to four quarters' (Section 6.2, p. 1613), and the usage scenario runs Q8-Q13. Strategic reading: the decision object is the structural composition of the firm's supplier and customer base, discussed with explicitly strategic vocabulary ('strategic priorities', 'strategic goals', 'strategic deliberation'), justified by reference to long-term buyer relationships [76] and interpreted through real options theory for market entry [30] versus NPV-based models [14,52] (Section 6.4, p. 1615). Upper-tactical reading: partnerships are formed and dissolved every simulated quarter, agents re-plan each turn, and the paper models the process as recurring edge add/remove/keep dynamics. Coded 'ambiguous'; R1 decision needed - the strategic reading appears the stronger of the two.
column31: The decision determines which firms constitute the focal firm's supply chain: agents issue collaboration Requests to create new supplier/customer relationships and termination Requests to dissolve existing ones, and counterparties accept or decline (Stages III and IV, p. 1608). The simulated outcome is a changed network topology, evaluated as edge add/remove/keep dynamics, and the authors generalise the mechanism as 'edge formation and deletion in social networks' (p. 1620). It determines what the network consists of, not how existing resources are utilised (no scheduling, inventory or flow decisions). NOTE: the authors never use the term 'system-configuring'; coded TRUE on the substance of the decision.
column33: No framework from the controlled vocabulary is cited. The paper's own theoretical scaffolding for partner selection is the integration of Multi-Criteria Decision-Making and Game Theory ('we address this gap by developing an integrated MCDM-GT framework to optimize partner selection with scenario-specific adaptability', Section 2.1, p. 1604), with MCDM weighted aggregation [55] and GT reviews [39] and signaling games [3] cited; real options theory [30] and NPV-based investment models [14,52] are invoked to interpret the usage-scenario outcome, and levels-of-autonomy work [18] frames the HITL design. These are decision-theoretic rather than strategic-planning-scope frameworks, so 'none' is a defensible alternative coding; R1 decision needed.
column34: SCSimulator models each firm in a supply chain as an autonomous LLM agent and simulates the evolution of supplier-customer relationships (partner selection) over discrete quarterly time steps, wrapped in an interactive visual analytics interface with human-in-the-loop intervention. BACKEND: (1) tri-dimensional company model - Network (temporal supplier/customer links), Feature (non-temporal e.g. industry; temporal e.g. patents, and expert-scored Operation/Technology/Reputation), Knowledge (global knowledge plus firm-specific natural-language context used as the agent's strategic foundation); firm performance quantified with network metrics such as number of collaborators and PageRank [58]. (2) Four-stage LLM request-response cycle per turn (Figure 2; full prompts Appendix A, Listings 1-5): Stage I Plan - the agent analyses its SC structure and Knowledge and emits plans with explicit Reasons and flags is_seek_collaboration / is_seek_suppliers; Stage II Query - plans are translated into partnership Constraints (industry_set plus per-feature weighted_scores) and a predefined query function retrieves and ranks a Candidate pool; Stage III Request - the agent selects targets and drafts persuasive, context-aware collaboration Requests (or termination Requests for reduction plans) with reasons and extra_info; Stage IV Reply - the agent evaluates incoming Requests against its own SC and active Plans for strategic alignment, feasibility and risk and accepts or declines with articulated Reasons. (3) SC Explain Model - per-firm predictive models trained on temporal SC data, inputs are node attributes and first-order network connections with VGAE-generated network embeddings [34], targets are firm-level performance metrics, user-selectable among Linear Regression, Lasso, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting; SHAP [48] provides global (which collaborators/attributes drive performance) and local (per-company) attribution, complementing the agents' qualitative CoT. (4) Horizon Extend Model - regression-based extrapolation of network-independent firm features beyond the last observed timestamp (same four model choices). FRONTEND: Upload Page where a conversational LLM agent maps the user's raw data onto the simulator's structured templates with real-time review/editing; Control Panel (performance metric, LLM model, SC Explain and Horizon Extend model selection with MSE/runtime box plots, editable Knowledge table, reference length, simulation turns); Global View (2D embedding timeline of SC evolution); Focus View (line-based egocentric 'berry orchard' visualisation where SHAP values position partners and encode influence, and collaboration stage is colour-encoded); Adjustment View (inspect and edit agent Knowledge, Plans, Candidates and incoming Requests; negate/add/delete, reset, apply modify); Simulation Path View (tree of simulation turns supporting branching and log export). Inputs: firm profiles and SC network data, natural-language Knowledge, simulation parameters. Outputs: simulated network evolution, agent plans/requests/replies with step-by-step reasons, SHAP attributions, forecast features, exportable simulation logs. Explicit decision-support function: a heuristic, exploratory 'what-if' sensemaking tool that expands the space of considered alternatives and makes implicit assumptions explicit - 'not positioned as an autonomous decision-making system' and a complement to, not a replacement for, rigorous analytical methods (pp. 1603, 1617, 1619).
column36: Three LLMs were compared as MAS backbone in the technical evaluation (Table 1, p. 1613): ChatGPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-flash and Qwen3-VL-Flash. Performance differences were limited, but ChatGPT-4o showed a small consistent advantage and 'is therefore selected as the default backbone model for subsequent experiments' (p. 1612); Figure 7 confirms ChatGPT-4o as the LLM agent in the usage scenario, and the user study reused the same setting. The same backbone serves all four agent stages and the conversational data-mapping agent on the Upload Page (no separate model reported). No temperature, context length or other decoding parameters are reported. Non-LLM model components: Variational Graph Autoencoder for network embeddings, and Linear/Lasso/Random Forest/Gradient Boosting regression for the SC Explain and Horizon Extend Models, with SHAP for attribution. Separately, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT and Gemini were used for code generation and manuscript editing and Nano Banana for one figure (Section 10) - tooling, not part of the artefact.
column40: All three backbone models were used as hosted commercial APIs; the authors state that 'the MAS in SCSimulator currently supports only basic commercial models' and that large-scale MAS is limited by 'the performance constraints of API-based LLM access' (Section 8.4.2, p. 1620), and point to small open LLMs [6] only as future work. AMBIGUITY: Qwen belongs to a family whose weights are generally released, and the schema lists Qwen under open-weight examples; if R1 treats Qwen3-VL-Flash as an open-weight model then 'mixed' applies. Coded 'N' because the paper reports only commercial API access and the default backbone (ChatGPT-4o) and Gemini-2.5-flash are unambiguously proprietary.
column42: No weight updates of any kind are reported. Behaviour is controlled entirely by persona-based prompt templates with strict JSON output formats, reproduced in full in Appendix A (Listing 1 CompanyInfo2Prompt, Listings 2-5 for Stages I-IV), together with user-editable Knowledge fields injected into the prompts. The authors note that 'our current LLM relies on persona-based prompts, which may lack specialized SC expertise' and propose knowledge bases, RAG and collaboration with experts to develop specialized LLMs as future work (Section 8.4.2, p. 1620). The only trained models are the non-LLM predictive components (VGAE, regressors).
column45: LLM-driven multi-agent simulation coupled with (a) trained predictive ML models plus SHAP-based XAI as a quantitative explanation layer over the agents' qualitative CoT, and (b) an interactive visual analytics frontend providing human-in-the-loop inspection, editing and branching ('simulate-check-adjust' cycle, p. 1620). Recorded under 'other' because the controlled vocabulary has no term for an LLM-MAS/predictive-model/XAI/visual-analytics hybrid; 'LLM+digital-twin' would over-claim (no digital twin, no physical asset model) and there is no solver.
column51: No optimization model, objective function, decision variables, constraints or solver appears in the system; the authors state that their emphasis 'distinguishes SCSimulator from traditional graph-based models, mathematical formulations, and visual analytics systems, and reflects an explicit trade-off: analytical rigor is relaxed in favor of expressive flexibility' (Section 8.1.1, p. 1617). The one formalized decision element that is implemented is MCDM-style weighted scoring: in Stage II each agent outputs an industry_set constraint and per-feature weighted_scores, and 'using predefined query functions, each agent retrieves and ranks a list of companies that best satisfy the weighted criteria' (p. 1608; Listing 3), i.e. weighted aggregation for candidate ranking without an optimality claim. Stages III-IV implement a request-accept/decline interaction that operationalises the game-theoretic side informally. The tradition the paper engages with is MCDM weighted aggregation [55], game theory [39], ML-MCDM hybrids [29,50,72] and MARL [80,87], and the stated aim is 'an integrated MCDM-GT framework to optimize partner selection' (p. 1604). Coded present at low formalization on the strength of the implemented weighted-criteria ranking plus the explicitly claimed MCDM-GT grounding; R1 may prefer optimization_tradition_present = FALSE / 'none' since nothing is optimized.

column53: No public dataset or benchmark. Self-constructed supply chain dataset built with the formative-study domain experts from real-world upstream and downstream paper packaging industry data: 35 anonymized firms observed over eight quarters (2023-2024); edges from public tendering and bidding relationships and node attributes from public firm profiles (sources given as cebpubservice.cn and gsxt.gov.cn); non-temporal features e.g. industry, temporal features e.g. patents; temporal attributes categorised and expert-scored along Operation, Technology and Reputation on a normalized 0-100 scale. The same dataset was reused for the expert evaluation and the user study for consistency. Authors cite the scarcity of high-quality SC data [23] as the reason for constructing a focused dataset; neither the dataset nor the code is stated to be available, and the paper notes the small domain-specific dataset limits generalizability (Section 8.4.1, p. 1620).

column113: SCSimulator was built and demonstrated end to end. Technically, the LLM-driven MAS reproduced observed next-quarter network evolution with moderate fidelity (best backbone ChatGPT-4o: ACC 72.43%, Precision 68.20%, Recall 59.75%, F1 63.11%; Gemini-2.5-flash and Qwen3-VL-Flash lower on all four), which the authors deem appropriate given that the tool targets plausible trajectories rather than prediction. Agent decision-making was highly self-consistent (Gwet's AC1 81.72-98.21%; 84.55-98.52% of firms in the high-CR band), attributed partly to the absence of prompt intervention and to imbalance in edge dynamics; medium-consistency firms were interpreted as structurally pivotal actors. Differences across the three LLMs were limited, so ChatGPT-4o was adopted as default backbone. In the expert evaluation (n=10) agent behaviour rated positively at every stage (plans 4.3, counterpart replies 4.7, Knowledge adherence 4.4 on a 5-point scale), with candidate selection weakest (3.7); qualitatively, agents were over-conservative without expert Knowledge and over-reactive with it. The usage scenario illustrated the intended sensemaking value rather than an optimum: a radical Knowledge directive caused firm 4838 to prune partners whose SHAP contributions were positive and to fail at customer acquisition, triggering a downward spiral that benefited rivals 6174 and 7437, whereas a conservative directive produced a first new partnership in Q12 (8610) and a second in Q13 (8660), a pattern the authors relate to real options theory. The user study (n=12) returned high usability, confidence and per-view effectiveness scores and low frustration and inconsistency, with mental demand, effort and especially learnability (1.67 / 1.33) as weak points; participants valued the SHAP layer as a 'quantitative anchor' for cross-validating agent reasoning and the combination of Global and Focus Views for reducing data overload, while noting realism limits of agent behaviour. Researchers used the system as a hypothesis sandbox and enterprise users as a decision-exploration tool. No baseline comparison, ablation or statistical testing is reported.
column116: Human-in-the-loop collaboration is a core design goal (DR6, DR7) and operates through several coupled mechanisms. (1) What-if / scenario exploration: the system 'foregrounds MAS-supported "what-if" exploration' so users 'can probe counterfactual configurations and alternative futures' (Section 8.1.1, p. 1617); the Adjustment View lets users inspect and rewrite an agent's Knowledge, expand Plans and Candidates and their dialogues, and intervene with Negate (refresh rejected collaborations), Add, Delete, Reset and Apply Modify at selected timestamps; every confirmed change is recorded with a new timestamp. (2) Branching exploration and traceability: the Simulation Path View renders simulation turns as a tree in which users switch between alternative paths and export logs (DR7). (3) Configuration-level steering via the Control Panel (performance metric, backbone LLM, explain/horizon models, reference length, simulation turns) and the Upload Page conversational mapping agent. (4) Expert oversight as a stated reliability condition: SCSimulator 'is not positioned as an autonomous decision-making system', with expert oversight 'a necessary condition for reliable use, providing a mechanism for validating assumptions, constraining agent behavior, and correcting undesirable trajectories' (Section 8.1.3, p. 1619). AMBIGUITY: the Apply Modify step and the requirement for expert confirmation of edits have approval-gate character, and Section 8.2.3 discusses autonomy levels and 'nudging' as boundary management; coded 'what-if-interface' because the dominant, explicitly named pattern is interactive scenario exploration rather than pre-execution approval. No uncertainty-triggered escalation to the human is reported.
column120: Domain knowledge is formalised in three coupled ways but never as an ontology or a semantic knowledge graph. (1) A tri-dimensional firm representation - Network (temporal supplier/customer links), Feature (non-temporal attributes such as industry; temporal attributes such as patents) and Knowledge (global knowledge, e.g. implicit interpretations of firm features, plus firm-specific strategic knowledge) - into which users' raw data are mapped via the simulator's structured templates with LLM assistance (Section 4.1.1, p. 1607; Figure 4). (2) An expert-derived measurement scheme: temporal firm attributes are categorised and scored by domain experts along three named dimensions, Operation, Technology and Reputation, on a normalized 0-100 scale, and firm importance is operationalised via network metrics (number of collaborators, PageRank [58]) following management research [33] (Sections 4.1.1, 5). (3) Prompt-level schemas that inject this structure into the agents (Listing 1 CompanyInfo2Prompt) and force strict JSON outputs with typed fields (plan, reason, is_seek_collaboration, industry_set, weighted_scores, is_chosen, is_accepted), i.e. a formalised decision-record schema (Appendix A). AMBIGUITY: the supply chain is represented as an attributed temporal graph and embedded with a VGAE, so 'knowledge-graph' could be argued, but no semantic relation types, axioms, graph query layer or ontology language are reported and the authors never use either term; the tacit expertise is deliberately externalised as free-text Knowledge rather than formal statements ('externalizing tacit expertise that is difficult to formalize', p. 1619). Coded 'other'; R1 may prefer 'knowledge-graph'.
column121: Tri-dimensional firm/SC schema (Network + Feature + Knowledge) with structured data templates, an expert-scored 0-100 Operation/Technology/Reputation attribute scheme and network-centrality performance metrics, plus typed JSON prompt schemas for agent plans, queries, requests and replies; free-text natural-language Knowledge fields carry the tacit domain expertise.
column124: Evaluation uses author-defined quantitative constructs together with standardised questionnaire instruments. Author-defined: simulated network evolution is scored against the observed next-step network as a binary link-prediction problem (ACC, Precision, Recall, F1), and decision consistency is operationalised as edge dynamics categorised add/remove/keep, aggregated with Gwet's AC1 [22] and with a purpose-defined firm-level consistency ratio (proportion of the most frequent decision category) banded into high (>0.8), medium (0.6-0.8) and low (<=0.6) levels (Section 5.1, p. 1612; Table 1). Standardised instruments: NASA-TLX for cognitive workload plus 5-point Likert batteries for usability and per-view effectiveness (Q1-Q17, Table 5) and a stage-wise 5-point Likert instrument for agent behaviour (Q1-Q4, Table 2). No standardised benchmark or published rubric exists for the task itself, and no baseline system is used. AMBIGUITY: because NASA-TLX and the Likert questionnaires are established instruments, R1 could instead code evaluation_framework_type = 'rubric'; coded 'domain-specific-metric' because the framework-specific CR/edge-dynamics and network-similarity metrics are what assess the artefact's core function.
column127: Score 2 - key steps described but gaps remain. Unusually strong on prompt transparency: all five agent prompt templates are reproduced verbatim in Appendix A (pp. 1623-1624), and the architecture is specified at component level (four-stage Plan/Query/Request/Reply cycle, tri-dimensional company model, VGAE embeddings [34], four selectable regressors, SHAP [48], five frontend views and their visual encodings, dataset construction and expert scoring procedure, evaluation protocol with 80 runs on 4 nodes and 4-quarter input windows). Missing for replication: no code or data availability statement (dataset is self-constructed and not stated to be released); exact backbone model versions beyond names and no decoding parameters (temperature, context length, retry/parsing behaviour); the Stage II 'predefined query functions' and ranking formula are not specified; VGAE and regression hyperparameters, training/validation splits and the target performance metric per model are not given; the labelling and criteria for the expert-scored 0-100 Operation/Technology/Reputation values are only sketched; expert-evaluation and user-study questionnaires are partially reported (Q18-Q20 open-ended items not analysed) and the 10 expert raters' task instructions are not given.
column129: Score 3 - implemented system plus quantitative evaluation. A working end-to-end system (LLM-driven MAS backend, predictive/SHAP explanation layer, Horizon Extend Model, five interactive views) was run on a real-world-derived dataset of 35 firms over 8 quarters and evaluated quantitatively across three backbone LLMs over 80 independent runs against observed network evolution (Table 1), complemented by an expert-based Likert evaluation (n=10, Table 2) and a task-based user study (n=12) with NASA-TLX, usability and effectiveness measures (Table 5) and a detailed usage scenario. This exceeds prototype-with-limited-evaluation. CAVEAT: there is no baseline or ablation, no statistical testing, a single-sector dataset, and the authors themselves characterise the validation as qualitative and the system as a proof-of-concept; if R1 codes validation_status = 'prototype', this dimension should be lowered to 2.
